name: Gish Gallop
hook: Well, actually, if you consider these fifteen points I'm about to list in ninety seconds…
oneLiner: Burying an opponent in a flood of weak claims faster than any can be answered.
deepDive: The Gish gallop wins by volume, not validity: fire off so many claims that no one can rebut them all in time, then declare the unanswered ones 'true.' It exploits an asymmetry — asserting a falsehood takes seconds, properly debunking one takes minutes.
howToSpot: A rapid barrage of many separate claims, too many to address at once
Quantity is doing the persuading, not the quality of any single point
Unanswered points get retroactively claimed as 'wins'

examples.text: In a debate, one side rattles off twelve dubious statistics in two minutes and demands the other refute every one.
examples.explanation: There's no time to debunk twelve claims, so most go unchallenged and are then treated as conceded.

examples.text: A comment reply lists twenty 'questions' the moment you make a single point.
examples.explanation: The volume is designed to overwhelm, not to genuinely inquire — answering one just triggers ten more.

examples.text: A thread drops a wall of links and claims, insisting you've 'lost' if you don't respond to all of them.
examples.explanation: The tactic converts your inability to reply to everything into a false victory.

refutation.title: Refuse the frame
refutation.text: Make clear you don't have to answer everything to be right.
refutation.comeback: I'm not going to chase twenty points at once. Let's take the strongest one properly.

refutation.title: Pick one and go deep
refutation.text: Choose the most load-bearing claim and dismantle it fully.
refutation.comeback: Let's start with your central claim. Here's exactly why it doesn't hold — one thing at a time.

refutation.title: Name the tactic
refutation.text: Point out the volume-over-substance strategy directly.
refutation.comeback: Flooding the conversation with claims isn't an argument. Slow down and defend one.

name: Moving the Goalposts
hook: Okay, you gave me one study — but one study means nothing. Show me ten. …Fine, but were they peer-reviewed in the last year?
oneLiner: Changing the standard of evidence the moment it's met, so it can never be satisfied.
deepDive: This is how someone never concedes: they set a standard for evidence, and the moment you meet it they raise the bar — not recent enough, not enough sources. The demand keeps retreating, so nothing is ever sufficient. Lock the criteria before you provide them.
howToSpot: A demand for evidence is met, then immediately replaced with a harder one
The standard keeps rising precisely as you keep satisfying it
No amount of evidence is ever treated as enough

examples.text: "Show me one expert who agrees." — You do. — "One doesn't count, show me the consensus."
examples.explanation: The bar jumps from 'one expert' to 'consensus' the instant the first bar is cleared.

examples.text: "If it ships by Friday I'll be impressed." — It ships Thursday. — "Well, is it bug-free though?"
examples.explanation: The success condition is redefined after it's met so the person never has to acknowledge it.

examples.text: "Prove it works in theory." — Done. — "Theory's easy, prove it in practice." — Done. — "At scale, though?"
examples.explanation: Each cleared standard is swapped for a tougher one, indefinitely.

refutation.title: Lock the criteria first
refutation.text: Get agreement on what would count as enough before providing it.
refutation.comeback: Before I dig up more, tell me exactly what would change your mind — and let's hold to that.

refutation.title: Name the shift
refutation.text: Point out the standard just moved.
refutation.comeback: That's a new requirement. I met the one you actually set — has your view changed?

refutation.title: Hold the original bar
refutation.text: Refuse to chase the retreating standard.
refutation.comeback: I answered the question you asked. I'm not going to keep clearing a bar that keeps moving.

name: Sealioning
hook: Sorry to bother you again — could you just cite a source for that? And that? And define that term? Just curious!
oneLiner: Feigning polite, endless requests for evidence to exhaust rather than to understand.
deepDive: Sealioning disguises harassment as polite curiosity: endless requests for evidence, definitions, sources for the sources — never satisfied, never engaging in good faith. The goal is to drain your energy until you snap, then look like the reasonable one. Answer once, then disengage.
howToSpot: Endless requests for sources, definitions, and clarification that never resolve
Exaggerated politeness paired with total refusal to engage the answers
The aim is clearly to exhaust you, not to learn anything

examples.text: After every answer, they reply 'Interesting — but could you provide a source for that too?' indefinitely.
examples.explanation: No answer is ever enough; the requests are designed to continue forever, not to reach understanding.

examples.text: They join a conversation uninvited demanding you 'just explain' a widely-known point, repeatedly.
examples.explanation: The feigned ignorance and politeness mask an intent to bog you down.

examples.text: Every source you give is met with 'and what's the source for that source?'
examples.explanation: The regress is bottomless by design — it's exhaustion dressed as diligence.

refutation.title: Answer once, then stop
refutation.text: Give a single good-faith response and decline to continue.
refutation.comeback: I've answered that. If you're genuinely curious, the information's there — I'm not doing this on loop.

refutation.title: Name the pattern
refutation.text: Call out that the questions aren't in good faith.
refutation.comeback: This isn't a real inquiry — you're not engaging with anything I say. I'm going to leave it here.

refutation.title: Set a boundary
refutation.text: State that you're disengaging, calmly.
refutation.comeback: I don't owe an endless stream of citations. We're done here.

name: Whataboutism
hook: You're criticising our record on this? What about what the other side did five years ago?
oneLiner: Deflecting criticism by pointing at someone else's unrelated wrongdoing.
deepDive: Whataboutism answers a criticism by pointing at someone else's unrelated wrong — 'but what about them?' — implying you must be flawless to have a point. But two things can both be bad; another's wrongdoing doesn't cancel the one actually being discussed.
howToSpot: Criticism is met with 'but what about...' pointing to a different wrong
The original issue is never actually addressed
The move implies the critic must be flawless to have a point

examples.text: "Your team missed the deadline." — "What about the other team's project last quarter?"
examples.explanation: Another team's failure doesn't address whether this deadline was missed.

examples.text: "This policy harms tenants." — "What about all the harm the previous government did?"
examples.explanation: Past harm elsewhere doesn't answer whether the current policy harms tenants now.

examples.text: "You broke the agreement." — "Well, what about the time you were late to everything?"
examples.explanation: An unrelated grievance is raised to avoid addressing the broken agreement.

refutation.title: Acknowledge, then redirect
refutation.text: Grant the other issue may matter, but hold the line.
refutation.comeback: That may be worth discussing separately — but it doesn't answer the point I raised.

refutation.title: Reject 'both or neither'
refutation.text: Point out that two things can both be true.
refutation.comeback: Both can be problems. One doesn't cancel the other. Let's stay on this one.

refutation.title: Return to the topic
refutation.text: Restate the original criticism plainly.
refutation.comeback: I'm still asking about the specific issue here. Can we address that?

name: False Equivalence
hook: A parking ticket, a bank robbery — they're both breaking the law, so who are you to judge?
oneLiner: Treating two things as morally or factually equal when the difference in scale or kind is huge.
deepDive: False equivalence flattens a huge difference by comparing two things that share only a surface feature — 'they both lied' equating a white lie with fraud. The similarity is trivial next to the differences it ignores. Grant the surface, then spell out the gap in scale.
howToSpot: Two very different things are treated as equivalent on a shared surface feature
Differences in scale, severity, or context are ignored
The comparison serves to minimise something serious or inflate something minor

examples.text: "Jaywalking and armed robbery are both crimes, so you can't lecture me about breaking rules."
examples.explanation: Both being 'crimes' ignores the vast difference in harm — the equivalence is only surface-deep.

examples.text: "Both candidates have been accused of things, so they're equally untrustworthy."
examples.explanation: Lumping a minor accusation with a serious one manufactures a balance that doesn't exist.

examples.text: "Skipping one meeting and abandoning the whole project are both 'not showing up.'"
examples.explanation: The phrase hides an enormous difference in consequence and intent.

refutation.title: Grant the surface, split the depth
refutation.text: Accept the shared feature, then name the difference.
refutation.comeback: Sure, technically both are X — but they differ enormously in scale. Here's how.

refutation.title: Quantify the gap
refutation.text: Make the difference in magnitude concrete.
refutation.comeback: One caused minor inconvenience, the other real harm. Treating them as equal erases that.

refutation.title: Reject the false balance
refutation.text: Refuse to accept manufactured equivalence.
refutation.comeback: These aren't comparable in the way you're implying, and lumping them together is the point.

name: Gaslighting
hook: I never said that. You're remembering it wrong — you always twist things. Are you sure you're okay?
oneLiner: Making someone doubt their own memory, perception, or sanity to gain control of the narrative.
deepDive: Gaslighting attacks not your argument but your confidence in reality — flat denial, rewritten events, questioning your memory or sanity — until you defer to their version. It's corrosive because it undermines the very tool you'd defend yourself with. At an interpersonal level it's a form of abuse.
howToSpot: Flat denial of things that clearly happened or were clearly said
Your memory, perception, or mental state is questioned instead of the facts
Over time you find yourself doubting what you plainly experienced

examples.text: "I never promised that — you're imagining things, you always do this."
examples.explanation: A clear commitment is denied and the target's memory attacked, shifting doubt onto them.

examples.text: "That meeting went fine, everyone agreed. You're the only one who saw a problem — think about that."
examples.explanation: A shared reality is rewritten and the target isolated as the unreliable one.

examples.text: "I didn't raise my voice. You're being oversensitive and dramatic, as usual."
examples.explanation: The event is denied and reframed as the target's defect rather than the speaker's behaviour.

refutation.title: Anchor to the record
refutation.text: Rely on external evidence rather than argued memory.
refutation.comeback: I've got it in writing. Let's look at what was actually said.

refutation.title: Name the behaviour
refutation.text: Identify the pattern of denial explicitly.
refutation.comeback: You're telling me something I clearly experienced didn't happen. That's not something I'll accept.

refutation.title: Seek outside perspective
refutation.text: Corroborate with others and, if it's a pattern, get support.
refutation.comeback: I trust what I saw, and others saw it too. I'm not going to argue about whether it was real.

name: JAQing Off (Just Asking Questions)
hook: I'm not saying it's rigged — I'm just asking why nobody will explain these 'irregularities.' Just asking questions!
oneLiner: Spreading insinuations by phrasing assertions as innocent questions.
deepDive: JAQing off ('just asking questions') smuggles a claim in as a question — 'I'm just asking why X' — planting the insinuation while keeping deniability, since nothing was actually asserted. The doubt is the point. Make the hidden claim explicit and hand the burden back.
howToSpot: 'Questions' that clearly imply a claim without stating it
The asker isn't interested in answers, only in raising suspicion
Deniability: 'I'm just asking' shields them from having to provide evidence

examples.text: "I'm not saying she's corrupt — I'm just asking why she won't address these rumours."
examples.explanation: The 'question' plants the accusation while dodging any burden to prove it.

examples.text: "Just curious — why does the data always seem to favour their side? Just asking."
examples.explanation: An insinuation of manipulation is delivered as innocent curiosity, immune to challenge.

examples.text: "I don't have a position, I'm only asking whether the vaccine has been properly tested."
examples.explanation: The doubt is the point; the question form provides cover from having to make and defend a claim.

refutation.title: Surface the hidden claim
refutation.text: State plainly what the question is implying.
refutation.comeback: It sounds like you're implying X. If so, say it directly and let's examine it.

refutation.title: Assign the burden
refutation.text: Point out that an implied claim still needs evidence.
refutation.comeback: If you're suggesting something, that's a claim — what's your evidence for it?

refutation.title: Answer, then test sincerity
refutation.text: Give a real answer and see if they engage.
refutation.comeback: Here's the actual answer to your question. Does that resolve it, or were you not really asking?

name: Motte and Bailey
hook: Everyone knows this group is dangerous. — That's a huge claim. — Well, I just mean we should be a bit cautious, obviously.
oneLiner: Advancing a bold claim, then retreating to a modest one when challenged — and back again.
deepDive: Named for a castle: advance a bold, hard-to-defend claim (the bailey), then retreat to a bland, obvious one (the motte) when challenged — and quietly return once the pressure lifts. The two get treated as interchangeable. Pin down which claim they're actually making.
howToSpot: A bold claim shrinks to a trivial one exactly when it's challenged
Once the challenge passes, the bold claim quietly returns
The modest and the extreme versions are treated as the same claim

examples.text: "Science is just another belief system." — Challenged — "I only mean scientists are human and can err." — Later, back to the strong claim.
examples.explanation: The defensible 'scientists can err' is used to shield the far bolder 'science is just belief.'

examples.text: "This company is evil." — Pushed — "I just meant no company is perfect." — Then returns to 'evil.'
examples.explanation: The trivial claim absorbs the criticism, then the extreme one resurfaces unharmed.

examples.text: "We should defund it entirely." — Challenged — "I'm only saying we should review the budget." — Later argues for full defunding again.
examples.explanation: 'Review the budget' is the motte protecting the bailey of 'defund entirely.'

refutation.title: Pin the claim
refutation.text: Ask them to commit to which version they're defending.
refutation.comeback: Which are you actually arguing — the strong version or the mild one? Pick one.

refutation.title: Block the retreat and return
refutation.text: Note when they shrink, and when they swing back.
refutation.comeback: You retreated to the mild claim when challenged, but now you're back to the strong one.

refutation.title: Separate the two
refutation.text: Address each claim distinctly.
refutation.comeback: The modest point is fine and I agree — but that's not the same as the bold claim, which I don't.

name: Concern Trolling
hook: As someone who really supports your cause, I'm worried these tactics are hurting you. Just trying to help!
oneLiner: Feigning support or worry to undermine a person or cause from the inside.
deepDive: A concern troll poses as a worried ally while steering you toward weakness — 'I support you, but your tactics are hurting you.' Framed as help, the advice always points toward doing less or giving up. Because it's 'support,' pushing back makes you look defensive.
howToSpot: Professed support paired with advice that always weakens your position
The 'concern' consistently nudges you toward doing less or giving up
Disagreeing is framed as you being defensive or ungrateful

examples.text: "I'm on your side, but honestly this campaign is making you look bad — maybe tone it down?"
examples.explanation: The 'help' pushes toward disarming, from someone whose real allegiance is unclear.

examples.text: "I want you to succeed, which is why I think you should stop pushing so hard."
examples.explanation: Framed as care, the advice reliably points toward reducing your effectiveness.

examples.text: "As a fan, I worry you're alienating people — you'd get further by staying quiet."
examples.explanation: Fake affiliation lends weight to counsel that would sideline you.

refutation.title: Judge the advice on merit
refutation.text: Evaluate whether the concern is actually sound.
refutation.comeback: I'll take the point on its merits — but 'do less' isn't obviously good advice here.

refutation.title: Ask for their stake
refutation.text: Probe where they actually stand.
refutation.comeback: Genuinely, where do you stand on this? Because the advice keeps pointing one direction.

refutation.title: Name the pattern
refutation.text: Call out fake concern when it's persistent.
refutation.comeback: Every suggestion you offer happens to weaken our position. I'm going to set the 'concern' aside.

name: Tone Policing
hook: I'd take your point more seriously if you weren't so emotional about it. Let's keep this civil.
oneLiner: Using politeness and 'tone' as a weapon to dismiss substance and control the conversation.
deepDive: Tone policing shifts scrutiny from what you said to how you said it, making a calmer delivery the price of being heard at all. The argument goes unanswered while the tone-policer looks like the reasonable one. It hinges on dismissal: engagement withheld, not merely requested.
howToSpot: The focus shifts to your tone or emotion instead of your point
Politeness or 'civility' is demanded as a precondition for engaging the substance
Legitimate frustration is reframed as the real problem

examples.text: "I can't discuss this while you're being so hostile — calm down and maybe I'll listen."
examples.explanation: Engagement is made conditional on tone, sidestepping the actual argument entirely.

examples.text: "There's no need to be emotional. Present it neutrally and then we'll see."
examples.explanation: The demand for composure shifts scrutiny from the claim to the claimant's manner.

examples.text: "If you really wanted to be taken seriously, you'd be more polite about it."
examples.explanation: Tone is used as a gatekeeping standard to avoid dealing with the substance.

validUses: Asking someone to stop personal insults **while still engaging the substance** is not tone policing
Noting that delivery is costing someone persuasive ground is strategic advice, not a dismissal of their claim
Disengaging from genuine abuse is legitimate — the fallacy is treating tone as a reason the argument is wrong

refutation.title: Decline the tone debate
refutation.text: Refuse to let delivery replace substance.
refutation.comeback: My tone isn't the issue — the argument is. Let's deal with what I actually said.

refutation.title: Separate manner from merit
refutation.text: Grant you can be blunt and still be right.
refutation.comeback: I can be frustrated and correct at the same time. Address the point, not the mood.

refutation.title: Name the deflection
refutation.text: Call out tone-policing as avoidance.
refutation.comeback: Focusing on how I said it, instead of what I said, is a way of not answering it.

name: Kafka Trapping
hook: Your denial only proves how deep the denial goes. An innocent person wouldn't be so defensive.
oneLiner: Framing any denial of an accusation as further proof of guilt.
deepDive: A Kafka trap is built so that denying the accusation confirms it — 'your defensiveness proves it,' and silence proves it too. No response counts as innocence; it's unfalsifiable by design. Name the structure: an accusation nothing could disprove is evidence of nothing.
howToSpot: Denying the accusation is treated as proof of it
There is no response — including silence — that would count as innocence
The accusation is structured so it can never be disproven

examples.text: "The fact that you're defending yourself so hard just shows I'm right."
examples.explanation: Self-defence is converted into evidence of guilt, leaving no valid way to respond.

examples.text: "Only someone hiding something would object to the question this strongly."
examples.explanation: Objecting is reframed as confirmation, so any pushback deepens the 'case.'

examples.text: "Your calm is suspicious, and if you got upset that'd prove it too."
examples.explanation: Every emotional state is pre-assigned as evidence — the trap has no exit.

refutation.title: Expose the structure
refutation.text: Point out that no answer could ever count as innocence.
refutation.comeback: You've set this up so nothing I say could clear me. That's not an argument, it's a trap.

refutation.title: Demand falsifiability
refutation.text: Ask what would count as disproof.
refutation.comeback: What response would you accept as me not being guilty? If there's none, the accusation is empty.

refutation.title: Return the burden
refutation.text: Insist the accuser provide actual evidence.
refutation.comeback: My denial isn't evidence. If you're making the charge, show something that actually supports it.

name: Playing the Victim
hook: I can't believe you're attacking me like this — after everything, you're the one making me feel awful.
oneLiner: Recasting yourself as the wronged party to deflect accountability and gain sympathy.
deepDive: When confronted, the person flips roles and becomes the injured party, so the conversation shifts from their accountability to your alleged cruelty. It often follows DARVO — Deny, Attack, Reverse Victim and Offender — hijacking sympathy to bury a valid concern.
howToSpot: The moment they're held accountable, they become the injured party
Roles are reversed — the person raising the issue is cast as the aggressor
Sympathy is used to bury the original concern, which goes unaddressed

examples.text: "You raised a real problem with my work." — "Wow, I try so hard and this is how you treat me?"
examples.explanation: The critique is reframed as an attack, shifting focus to the speaker's hurt instead of the problem.

examples.text: "You didn't follow through on your commitment." — "I'm always the bad guy, aren't I? Everyone blames me."
examples.explanation: Accountability is dodged by casting the self as a perpetual victim.

examples.text: "That comment was hurtful." — "So now I'm the villain for having feelings? You're the one hurting me."
examples.explanation: Offender and offended are swapped so the original harm is never addressed.

refutation.title: Acknowledge, then hold the line
refutation.text: Note real feelings without dropping the issue.
refutation.comeback: I don't want to upset you — and the original concern still needs addressing.

refutation.title: Name the role-reversal
refutation.text: Point out the roles have been flipped.
refutation.comeback: We started with something you did, and now somehow I'm the problem. Let's go back.

refutation.title: Separate feelings from facts
refutation.text: Distinguish being upset from being wronged.
refutation.comeback: You can feel hurt and still be the one accountable here. Those are different things.

name: Selective Outrage
hook: This is an absolute scandal! …No, I had nothing to say when our own side did the exact same thing.
oneLiner: Expressing intense outrage over an act only when the 'other side' does it.
deepDive: Selective outrage applies a standard inconsistently — fury when an opponent acts, silence or excuses when an ally does the same. The principle turns out to be a weapon of convenience, not a real conviction. Line the two cases up side by side and the double standard shows.
howToSpot: Fierce outrage at one side's act, silence or excuses for the same act by the other
The 'principle' is only ever invoked against opponents
Lining up the two cases reveals a double standard

examples.text: "This gaffe is disqualifying!" — but the identical gaffe by their own candidate went unmentioned.
examples.explanation: The standard is applied only to the opponent, exposing the outrage as partisan, not principled.

examples.text: "Cronyism is a disgrace when they do it" — while their own side's cronyism draws no comment.
examples.explanation: The principle is real only when it's convenient; the inconsistency reveals the motive.

examples.text: "Breaking the rules is unforgivable" — said by someone who defended rule-breaking on their own team.
examples.explanation: The same act triggers fury or forgiveness depending purely on who did it.

refutation.title: Line up the parallel
refutation.text: Present the equivalent case they ignored.
refutation.comeback: You were furious here — but silent when your own side did the same. What changed?

refutation.title: Test the principle
refutation.text: Ask whether the standard applies universally.
refutation.comeback: If this is really about the principle, it should apply to everyone. Does it?

refutation.title: Separate the act from the actor
refutation.text: Judge the action on consistent terms.
refutation.comeback: Either the act is wrong regardless of who does it, or the outrage isn't about the act.
